title: The Apology
author: Plato
openingText: How you, O Athenians, have been affected by my accusers, I cannot tell; but I know that they almost made me forget who I was — so persuasively did they speak; and yet they have hardly uttered a word of truth. But of the many falsehoods told by them, there was one which quite amazed me — I mean when they said that you should be upon your guard and not allow yourselves to be deceived by the force of my eloquence.
about:
The Apology is Plato's account of Socrates's defense at his trial in 399 BCE. Socrates has been accused of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens. The Apology is his speech: he refuses to apologize in the modern sense, refuses to back down, and explains his philosophical method — questioning everyone he meets, looking for wisdom and not finding it. The jury finds him guilty. He is sentenced to death by drinking hemlock.

The text is short — a few hours' reading — and it is the founding document of Western philosophy as a way of life. It is also the founding example of someone choosing principle over survival when the choice was real.

angleCards.title: Why he refuses to beg.
angleCards.text: Socrates is 70, and he knows the jury. A few tears and a show of regret would probably have saved him. He refuses. I want to read the Apology asking what in his philosophy makes begging impossible — and whether that principle holds up under pressure.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand why Socrates refuses to beg for his life — what his philosophy actually demands of him at the moment of his death, and whether that choice is wisdom or pride.

angleCards.title: The examined life.
angleCards.text: "The unexamined life is not worth living." It is the most famous line in Western philosophy and it is said by a man about to die for living it. I want to read the Apology asking what examination actually requires — and what Socrates thought most people were missing.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to take the "examined life" argument seriously — that the unexamined life is not worth living — and test it against my own life and the lives described in the text.

angleCards.title: Socrates as gadfly.
angleCards.text: He describes himself as a gadfly attached to a great but sluggish horse — Athens — whom the gods sent to sting it into wakefulness. I want to read the Apology as a warning about what societies do to their irritants, and whether the gadfly metaphor still holds.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Apology as a political text — what happens when a society silences its most honest critic — and ask what Socrates as gadfly means for how we think about dissent.

angleCards.title: Athens on trial.
angleCards.text: Socrates is technically the defendant. But his speech keeps turning the question back on the jury — what does it say about you that you want this? I want to read the Apology as a double trial, and ask which party comes out worse.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Apology as an accusation of Athens — not just a defence of Socrates — and ask whether the trial is really about him or about what kind of city Athens wants to be.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: Seventy years old, barefoot, famously ugly, and completely unintimidated. He spent his life questioning Athenians about whether they really knew what they claimed to know. He has been found inconvenient. He will not stop.

cast.name: Meletus
cast.description: The young poet who formally brings the charges — impiety and corrupting the youth. Socrates cross-examines him in the middle of his own defence speech and reveals that Meletus hasn't thought carefully about what he's actually claiming.

cast.name: Anytus
cast.description: The real power behind the prosecution — a democratic politician who considers Socrates a threat to the restored democracy. He is not mentioned as often as Meletus, but Socrates implies he is the one who matters.

cast.name: The Jury of 501
cast.description: Five hundred and one ordinary citizens of Athens who vote on guilt and sentence. Socrates addresses them throughout — sometimes respectfully, sometimes with pointed irony. They vote to execute him by a majority of 60. Plato was in the room.

cast.name: The Oracle at Delphi
cast.description: The oracle declared that no one was wiser than Socrates. Socrates was confused — he knew he knew nothing. He spent decades interviewing people who claimed wisdom and discovering they didn't have it. This is why Athens hates him.

cast.name: Athens
cast.description: The world's first democracy, fresh from civil war, anxious about its identity. It executes its most famous philosopher for asking uncomfortable questions. Socrates predicts this will be remembered as a mistake. He was right.

whyItMatters.title: The Examined Life
whyItMatters.body: Socrates says: "the unexamined life is not worth living." The line is one of the most quoted in philosophy. The Apology is the argument for it — given by a man who knows he will be killed for living that way.

whyItMatters.title: Standing By the Argument
whyItMatters.body: Socrates does not flatter the jury. He does not minimize his views. He does not promise to stop. The Apology is a portrait of someone refusing to live by lying about what he thinks, and accepting the cost.

whyItMatters.title: The Founding Death
whyItMatters.body: Socrates's death is the founding martyrdom of philosophy. Christianity has Christ; philosophy has Socrates. Reading the Apology is reading the trial that has shaped the way philosophers see themselves for two and a half millennia.
